https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.question: Does success demonstrate that its recipient deserves the advantages it brings?
https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.thesis: The Zhuangzi-inspired critique treats individual accomplishment as inseparable from circumstance, opportunity and relationships.
https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.argument: Skill and effort matter, but they are exercised in environments nobody creates alone. If circumstances contribute to success, treating achievement as pure moral desert ignores luck and interdependence.
https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.intellectual_background: Zhuangzi is a foundational classical Daoist text; the essay places its stories alongside contemporary debates over meritocracy and deservingness.
https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.example: Two equally industrious students encounter very different teachers, health, family resources and opportunities; their eventual outcomes cannot be attributed to effort alone.
https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.strongest_objection: Recognizing luck can understate genuine skill and the incentives created by rewarding effort.
https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.possible_response: Acknowledge effort and competence without claiming outcomes measure intrinsic worth or justify unlimited inequality.
https://aeon.co/essays/zhuangzi-and-the-.implications: Institutions can reward useful work while remaining attentive to structural access and the dignity of those who lose.
unresolved_questions: How should effort and luck influence reward?
